history.heading: Early kingdoms and Malacca
paragraphs: The Malay Peninsula and northern Borneo have been inhabited for tens of thousands of years; the Niah Caves in Sarawak hold some of the oldest human remains in Southeast Asia. Early Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms, such as Kedah, traded with India and China.
Around 1400 the Malacca Sultanate was founded and became the region's greatest trading port, controlling the Strait of Malacca. Its rulers adopted Islam, which spread across the Malay world.

history.heading: European colonialism
paragraphs: Portugal captured Malacca in 1511, followed by the Dutch in 1641. Britain established Penang (1786), Singapore (1819) and Malacca as the Straits Settlements and gradually extended control over the Malay states. British North Borneo and Sarawak, ruled by the "White Rajahs" of the Brooke family, were also under British influence.
Tin mining and rubber plantations attracted large numbers of Chinese and Indian workers, creating a multi-ethnic society. Japan occupied the region from 1941 to 1945.

history.heading: Independence and federation
paragraphs: After a communist insurgency known as the Malayan Emergency, the Federation of Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957 under Tunku Abdul Rahman. Malaysia was formed in 1963 with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore; Singapore left in 1965.

Ethnic riots in 1969 led to the New Economic Policy, which favoured the Malay majority. Mahathir Mohamad, prime minister from 1981 to 2003, oversaw rapid modernisation. The Barisan Nasional coalition governed from independence until its first defeat in 2018, amid the 1MDB corruption scandal. Anwar Ibrahim became prime minister in 2022.

culture.heading: A multicultural nation
paragraphs: Malays and other indigenous groups (Bumiputera) make up about 70 percent of the population, with large Chinese and Indian communities. Malay is the national language, and English, Chinese dialects and Tamil are widely spoken. Islam is the official religion, and Buddhism, Christianity and Hinduism are also practised.
Major festivals include Hari Raya Aidilfitri, Chinese New Year, Deepavali and Christmas, celebrated with "open houses" welcoming people of all backgrounds.

culture.heading: Food and landmarks
paragraphs: Malaysian cuisine blends Malay, Chinese and Indian influences: nasi lemak (coconut rice), the national dish, satay, laksa, roti canai and char kway teow. The Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004. Badminton is the most popular sport.

politics.heading: Federal constitutional monarchy
paragraphs: Malaysia is a federal constitutional monarchy. A unique rotating system elects the king (Yang di-Pertuan Agong) every five years from among the nine hereditary Malay rulers. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the elected Dewan Rakyat.
Politics is shaped by ethnicity and religion, and by debates over Malay privileges, Islam's role and corruption. Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo have special autonomy.

economy.heading: Upper-middle-income economy
paragraphs: Malaysia has one of the most developed economies in Southeast Asia. It is a major exporter of electronics and semiconductors (Penang is a key hub for chip assembly and testing), palm oil, natural gas, petroleum and rubber gloves. Data centres have attracted large investments.
Tourism is significant. The currency is the ringgit. Malaysia aims to reach high-income status while reducing inequality and dependence on commodities.
